label: thm:oswhardness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:oswhardness}
    No OSW algorithm (randomized or fractional) is  $(\nicefrac{1}{2}+\varepsilon)$-competitive under adversarial arrivals, for any constant $\varepsilon>0$. This holds unconditionally, regardless of computation~time.

    No OSW algorithm (randomized or fractional) is  $(1-\nicefrac{1}{e}+\varepsilon)$-competitive under known i.i.d.~(even uniform) arrivals, for any constant $\varepsilon>0$, regardless of computation time.

label: def:stochastic-coverage-fn
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:stochastic-coverage-fn}
    Let $\mathbf{X}\in \{0,1\}^\mathcal{U}$ be a random binary vector (with possibly correlated entries). Then the \emph{probability-coverage function} $h_{\mathbf{X}}:2^{\mathcal{U}}\to \mathbb{R}^+$ is given by $$h_{\mathbf{X}}(S)\triangleq \Pr\left[\bigvee_{e\in S}(X_e=1)\right].$$
head: environment

label: lem:stochastic-coverage
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:stochastic-coverage}
Any probability-coverage function $h_{\mathbf{X}}$ is a weighted coverage function, and hence a normalized, non-negative monotone submodular function.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Omega$ be the discrete probability space over which $\mathbf{X}$ is defined. For each item $e\in \mathcal{U}$, define
\[
A_e\triangleq \{\omega\in\Omega : X_e(\omega)=1\}.
\]
Next, define (non-negative) weights $w(\omega)\triangleq \Pr[\{\omega\}]$ for each atom $\omega\in\Omega$. Then for any set $S\subseteq \mathcal{U}$,
\begin{align*}
h_{\mathbf{X}}(S) & =\Pr\left(\bigcup_{e\in S}A_e\right)=\sum_{\omega\in\cup_{e\in S}A_e}w(\omega)
.\qedhere
\end{align*}
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: If the probability space $\Omega$ over which $\mathbf{X}$ is defined is a uniform distribution over its atoms, then $h_{\mathbf{X}}$ is an \emph{unweighted} coverage function.

label: lem:closed-form
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:closed-form}
    Fix buyer $i\in [n]$ and its partition $\mathcal{P}_i$ of $\mathcal{U}_i\subseteq \mathcal{U}$. The value of any set $S\subseteq \mathcal{U}$ for~$i$~is $$f_i(S)\triangleq 1-\prod_{P\in \mathcal{P}_i}\left(1-\frac{|S\cap P|}{k}\right).$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For each part $P\in \mathcal{P}_i$ we have $\sum_{e\in P} X_e= 1$. But since $\Pr[X_e=1]=1/k$ for all $e\in \mathcal{U}_i$, we then have that $\Pr\left[\bigwedge_{e\in P\cap S} (X_e=0)\right] = 1-|S\cap P|/k$. The formula then follows from independence across parts and $X_e=0$ for all items $e\in \mathcal{U}\setminus \mathcal{U}_i$.
head: environment

label: cor:closed-form
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:closed-form}
    Fix buyer $i\in [n]$ and bundle $S\subseteq \mathcal{U}$. If $|S\cap P|=k$ for any part $P\in \mathcal{P}_i$, then $f_i(S)=1$. 
    Conversely, if    
    $|S\cap P|\leq 1$ for all parts $P\in \mathcal{P}_i$, then $f_i(S)=1-(1-1/k)^{|S\cap \mathcal{U}_i|}$.

title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:closed-form-frac}

label: lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We say item $e$ is \emph{good} for buyer $i$ if a copy of $e$ is the last arrival from part $P\in \mathcal{P}_i$~containing~$e$. Otherwise, $e$ is \emph{bad} for $i$.
    Let $B\triangleq \{(i,e) \mid e \textrm{ is bad for $i$}\}$ be the set of bad buyer-item pairs. 
    Trivially, the vector $\mathbf{z}\triangleq \mathbf{x}_{\mid B}$ satisfies $\mathbf{0}\leq\mathbf{z}\leq \mathbf{x}$. Moreover, since $x_{i,e}=z_{i,e}$ for all items $e$ other than the last arriving item in any part $P\in \mathcal{P}_i$, the vectors $\mathbf{x}$ and $\mathbf{z}$ satisfy Property  \eqref{prop:no-repeates}.

    Next, for buyer $i$ and time $t$ with arrival $\sigma_t=e\in P\in \mathcal{P}_i$, let $F_{i,t}$ be an indicator variable for the event that some other item $e'\in \mathcal{P}\setminus \{e\}$ arrives at some later time $t'>t$.
    With this notation, since $(i,e)$ is bad iff $F_{i,t}=1$ for all $t$ for which $\sigma_t =e$,
    and since $x_{i,e}=\sum_{t} y_{i,t} \cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]$, 
    \begin{align*}
    z_{i,e}  
    & = \sum_t y_{i,t} \cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t =e] \cdot \mathds{1}[\forall t:\;  \sigma_t =e \Longrightarrow F_{i,t}=1] \\
    & \leq \sum_t y_{i,t} \cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t =e] \cdot  F_{i,t}.
    \end{align*}
    On the other hand, for any $i,t$, and possible arrival $\sigma_t=e$, by union bound and \Cref{fact:parameters},
    $$\Pr[F_{i,t}=1] \leq (m-t)\cdot \frac{k-1}{u} \leq m\cdot \frac{k}{u} = O(nk^2/u) = o(1).$$
    Moreover, since future arrivals are independent of past and present arrivals and the present choices of the online algorithm, we have that 
    $F_{i,t}$ is independent of $y_{i,t}\cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]$.
    Therefore,  
    $$\mathbb{E}[y_{i,t} \cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]\cdot F_{i,t}] = \mathbb{E}[y_{i,t}\cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]]\cdot \mathbb{E}[F_{i,t}] = \mathbb{E}[y_{i,t}\cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]]\cdot o(1).$$
    Property \eqref{prop:z-small} follows, as $\sum_{i,t}y_{i,t}\leq m = nk$ always (since $\sum_i y_{i,t}\leq 1$ for each time $t\in [m]$): 
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[\|z\|_1]=\sum_{i}\sum_e \mathbb{E}[z_{i,e}] & \leq \sum_i \sum_e \sum_{t} \mathbb{E}[y_{i,t}\cdot \mathds{1}[\sigma_t=e]]\cdot \mathbb{E}[F_{i,t}] \leq nk \cdot o(1) = o(nk). \qedhere 
    \end{align*}
head: environment

label: lem:online-iid-allocation-structure
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For buyer $i$, let $B_i\triangleq \{e\mid (x-z)_{i,e} = 0\}$ and 
    let $A_i\triangleq \mathcal{U}\setminus B_i$. 
    
    First, by Property \eqref{prop:z-small} of the hypothesis, we have that $\mathbb{E}[\sum_i \|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid B_i}\|_1] \leq \mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{z}\|_1]=o(nk)$.
    So, since $f_i(\{e\})=1/k$ for each $e\in \mathcal{U}$, and $f_i$ is submodular and hence subadditive, we have that 
    $$\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid B_i})\right] \leq 1/k\cdot o(nk) = o(n).$$

    On the other hand, by Property \eqref{prop:no-repeates} of the hypothesis and \Cref{cor:closed-form-frac}, 
    $$\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid A_i})\right] \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid A_i}\|_1}\right)\right] \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i\left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}}\|_1\right)\right].$$

    
    The lemma follows, as $f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\leq f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid A_i}) + f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}_{\mid B_i})$ by subadditivity of $f^+$ (\Cref{subadditivity}).

title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:online-iid-allocation-value}
    For this i.i.d.~OSW instance, any (fractional or randomized) OSW algorithm attains expected social welfare at most $n(1-(1-1/k)^k+o(1)).$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For fractional algorithms, this follows from \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition,lem:online-iid-allocation-structure} and concavity of the univariate function $g(z)=(1-(1-1/k)^z)$, and $\sum_i \|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1 = \|\mathbf{x}\|_1\leq nk$.
    The consequence for randomized algorithms then follows from \Cref{fractional->fact:random}.

title: Lemma

\label{lem:offline-iid-allocation}
    For this i.i.d.~OSW instance, the offline \Cref{alg:offline-OSW} allocates an expected $n(1-o(1))$ of the buyers $i$ a bundle $S_i$ containing an entire part $P$ of the partition $\mathcal{P}_i$, i.e., $|P\cap S_i|=k$. Consequently, by \Cref{cor:closed-form}, $OPT(SW)\geq n(1-o(1))$.

label: cla:many-distinct-types
title: Fact
body_md:
\label{cla:many-distinct-types}
        Let $D$ be the number of distinct arrived items (i.e., $D=|S|$ after Line \ref{offline-OSW:init}). Then $$\mathbb{E}[D]\geq nk(1-o(1)).$$
head: environment

title: Proof

label: cla:part-contained-in-large-sample-by-bday-paradox
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{cla:part-contained-in-large-sample-by-bday-paradox}
        Fix an item set $S\subseteq \mathcal{U}$ of size $s\geq \max\{2k,\;2u^{1-1/k}(10k\ln  n)^{1/k}\}$. Then, for any buyer $i$,
        with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$ over the randomness of $\mathcal{P}_i$, at least one part $P
        \in \mathcal{P}_i$ is contained in~$S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $D$ be the number of distinct items after  Line \ref{offline-OSW:init}  of \Cref{offline-OSW:init}.    
    Fix some $s=o(n)$ as in \Cref{cla:part-contained-in-large-sample-by-bday-paradox}. (Note that such an $s=o(n)$ exists, by \Cref{fact:parameters}.)
    By \Cref{cla:many-distinct-types}, since $D\leq nk$, we have that $\mathbb{E}[nk-D]\leq o(nk)$, and so by Markov's inequality, 
    $$\Pr[D\leq s] = \Pr[nk-D\geq nk-s] \leq \frac{o(nk)}{nk-s} = o(1).$$
    Therefore, again using \Cref{cla:many-distinct-types},
    \begin{align*}
    \mathbb{E}[D \cdot \mathds{1}[D\geq s]] & = \mathbb{E}[D \mid D\geq s] \Pr[D\geq s] \\
    & \geq \mathbb{E}[D]\Pr[D\geq s] = nk(1-o(1)).
    \end{align*}
    We lower bound the offline algorithm's gain, only accounting for its value when $D\geq s$, on which we condition below.
    
    While \Cref{alg:offline-OSW} iterates through the first $\lfloor D/k-s/k\rfloor$ buyers, it allocates at most $D-s$ items, as it allocates each buyer at most $k$ items. Therefore, for each of these first buyers, if $D\geq s$, then at least $s$ distinct items are not yet allocated when \Cref{alg:offline-OSW} considers these buyers.
    So, by \Cref{cla:part-contained-in-large-sample-by-bday-paradox} and the principle of deferred decision \cite{mitzenmacher2017probability} (specifically, drawing $\mathcal{P}_i$ only when this partition is first inspected), each of the first $\lfloor D/k-s/k\rfloor $ buyers is allocated one of their parts with probability at least $1-n^{-10}$. 
    Therefore, by union bound, all these first $\lfloor D/k-s/k\rfloor \leq n$ buyers are allocated one of their parts in its entirety with probability at least $1-n^{-9}$. Consequently, and combined with $\mathbb{E}[D \cdot \mathds{1}[D\geq s]]\geq nk(1-o(1))$ the expected number of buyers allocated a bundle containing one of their parts is at least $\mathbb{E}[D/k\cdot \mathds{1}[D\geq s]]-s/k-1-n^{-8} \geq n(1-o(1))$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By \Cref{lem:offline-iid-allocation}, we have that
    \begin{align*}
    OPT(SW) & \geq n(1-o(1)).
    \end{align*}
    In contrast, by \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-value}, any online  algorithm $ALG$ has 
    $$ALG(SW) \leq n(1-(1-1/k)^k + o(1)).$$
    The theorem then follows, as $1-(1-\nicefrac{1}{k})^k+o(1) = 1-1/e+o(1)$ since $k = \omega(1)$ (by \Cref{fact:parameters}).

label: lem:offline-adv-allocation
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $r\in [c]$, consider the i.i.d.~OSW instance consisting of the $n/c$ buyers in $D^{(r)}$ and the $nk/c$ items drawn i.i.d.~from $\mathcal{U}^{(r)}$ in round $r$. Since $c$ is constant, the asymptotic relations of \Cref{fact:parameters} continue to hold for this instance's number of buyers, $n'=n/c$, universe size, $u'=u/c$, and number of arrivals per buyer, $m'/n'=k'=k$. Consequently, \Cref{lem:offline-iid-allocation} holds for this instance.
    We conclude that there exists an (offline) allocation, allocating all arrivals from $\mathcal{U}^{(r)}$ to the buyers in $D^{(r)}$ with expected social welfare $(n/c)(1-o(1))$.
    Combining these (buyer-disjoint) allocations for $r=1,\dots,c$ yields an offline allocation with expected social welfare $\sum_{r=1}^c (n/c)\cdot (1-o(1)) = n(1-o(1))$.
head: environment

label: lem:online-adv-structure
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For any $r\in [c]$, consider the i.i.d.~OSW instance consisting of the $(c-r+1)(n/c)$ active buyers in round $r$,  $A^{(r)}\triangleq \bigcup_{j\geq r} D^{(j)}$, and the $nk/c$ items drawn i.i.d.~from $\mathcal{U}^{(r)}$ in round $r$.
    Since $c$ is constant, the asymptotic relations of \Cref{fact:parameters} continue to hold for this instance's universe size, $u'=u/c$, 
    part size $k$, 
    number of buyers, $n'=(c-r+1)(n/c) \in [n/c,n]$, 
    and an upper bound $\tilde{m}=n'k$ on the number of arrivals $m' = nk/c \in [n'k/c,n'k]$. 
    Consequently, this input is a prefix of $m'\leq \tilde{m}$ arrivals of an input considered by
    \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition}. 
    Therefore, the allocation of $ALG$ on the entire instance restricted to  these first $m'$ arrivals of round $r$ can be seen as an OSW algorithm run on the instance with parameters $u',n',k,\tilde{m}$, by simulating $ALG$ on the first $m'$ arrivals and then allocating no further items.\footnote{Note that  arrivals and buyers' partitions in round $r$ are independent of the information revealed in previous rounds, and so this information does not help $ALG$ predict the instance of round $r$. Therefore, after seeing rounds $1,\dots,r-1$, the above algorithm is an online algorithm when restricted to round $r$.}
    Therefore, the allocation vector $\mathbf{x}(r)$ of $ALG$ restricted to the items of round $r$ (which are disjoint from the items of other rounds) decomposes into $\mathbf{x}(r)=(\mathbf{x}(r)-\mathbf{z}(r))+\mathbf{z}(r)$ as in \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition}.
    Since each part of $\mathcal{P}_i$ is contained in a single round's item set $\mathcal{U}^{(j)}$, this implies a decomposition of $\mathbf{x}=\sum_{r=1}^c\mathbf{x}(r)$, the overall fractional allocation of $ALG$, into $\mathbf{x}=(\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{z})+\mathbf{z},$ for $\mathbf{z}\triangleq \sum_r \mathbf{z}(r)$ satisfying $\mathbf{0}\leq \mathbf{z}\leq \mathbf{x}$, as well as Property \eqref{prop:z-small},
    $\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{z}\|_1]=\sum_r \mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{z}(r)\|_1] = c\cdot o(nk) = o(nk)$, and 
    Property \eqref{prop:no-repeates}.

body_md:
\label{lem:online-adv-unbalanced}

    $$\mathbb{E}[\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1] \leq k\cdot \left(H_c - H_{c-r}\right),$$

label: lem:online-adv-allocation
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an online algorithm $ALG$. By \Cref{lem:online-adv-structure}, the fractional allocation $\mathbf{x}$ output by $ALG$ decomposes as in \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition}.
    Therefore, $ALG$'s social welfare, $(\dag)\triangleq ALG(SW) = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i f_i^+(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\right]$ satisfies, by \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-structure}, Jensen's inequality and \Cref{lem:online-adv-unbalanced}:
    \begin{align*}
         (\dag) & = \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i\in [n]} \left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1}\right)\right] + o(n)   \\
        \\ & = \frac{n}{c}\cdot \sum_{r=1}^c  \mathbb{E}_{i\sim \mathrm{Uni}(D^{(r))}}  \left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1]}\right) + o(n) \\
        & \leq \frac{n}{c}\cdot \sum_{r=1}^{c} \left(1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k\cdot \left(H_c-H_{c-r}\right)}\right) + o(n).
    \end{align*}
    From here on out, upper bounding the above by $n(\nicefrac{1}{2}+\nicefrac{1}{(2c)}+o(1))$ follows by standard algebra, similarly to the analysis in \cite{kapralov2013online} for computational hardness of OSW. See \Cref{app:hardness} for the full proof.

label: def:concave-extension
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:concave-extension}
	Given an arrival sequence $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\dots, \sigma_m)\in \mathcal{U}^m$, let $\mathcal{E}\triangleq [n]\times\mathcal{U}$ denote the ground set of buyer--item pairs, and let $m_e(\sigma)\triangleq |\{t\in [m] \mid \sigma_t=e\}|$ denote the number of arrivals of item $e\in \mathcal{U}$. We define the set of feasible allocations as the partition matroid:
	\[
	\mathcal{M}_\sigma \triangleq \left\{ S \subseteq \mathcal{E} \;\middle|\; \left|S \cap \bigl([n]\times\{e\}\bigr)\right| \le m_e(\sigma) \text{ for every } e \in \mathcal{U} \right\}.
	\]
	For any allocation $S\subseteq \mathcal{E}$, let $S_i=\{e\in \mathcal{U} \mid (i,e)\in S\}$ denote the set of items assigned to buyer $i$. The \emph{total submodular welfare} of $S$ is:
	\[
	g(S) \triangleq \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(S_i).
	\]
	For a fractional allocation $\mathbf{x}$ in the matroid polytope $\mathrm{conv}(\mathcal{M}_\sigma)\triangleq \mathrm{conv}\{\mathds{1}_S \mid S\in \mathcal{M}_\sigma\}$ (which contains the output of any fractional OSW algorithm on $\sigma$), the \emph{concave closure of OSW} on $\sigma$ is defined as:
	\[
	g_{\sigma}^+(\mathbf{x}) \triangleq \max \left\{ \sum_{S\in\mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S \cdot g(S) \;\middle\vert\; \sum_{S\in\mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S = 1,\ \mathbf{\alpha} \ge \mathbf{0},\ \sum_{S\ni(i,e)} \alpha_S = x_{i,e} \ \forall (i,e)\in \mathcal{E} \right\}.
	\]

label: fact:g+upper-bound
title: Fact
head: environment

label: obs1
title: Observation
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: As demonstrated in the proof below, the alternative extensions $g^1$ and $g^2$ essentially ``linearize'' the objective function for our construction. In the adversarial setting, the linearization reduces the evaluation of $g^1$ and $g^2$ at the solution that splits each arriving item equally among all active buyers to analyzing the performance of the classic Water-Filling (or Balance) algorithm on the standard upper-triangular instance for online $b$-matching~\citep{kalyanasundaram2000optimal}, yielding a $(1-\nicefrac1e)$-fraction of the offline optimum.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first show the upper bound on $\mathbb{E}[g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)]$. Because $\mathbf{x}^*$ can be viewed as the output of a trivial online algorithm that splits every arriving item equally among all buyers, the general upper bound for online algorithms (Lemma \ref{lem:online-iid-allocation-value} and Fact \ref{fact:g+upper-bound}) implies that $\mathbb{E}[g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x}^*)] \le (1-1/e)n + o(n)$. 
	
	Next, we lower bound $\mathbb{E}[g^1(\mathbf{x}^*)]$. Let $\varepsilon = e^{-n}$, and let $A(\sigma)\triangleq \{e\in \mathcal{U} \mid m_e(\sigma)\geq 1\}$ denote the set of arrived item types. We construct a candidate solution $\mathbf{z}$ for the linear program defining $g^1$ by setting $z_{i,e} = (1-\varepsilon)\cdot \frac{1}{n} = \frac{1-\varepsilon}{n}$ for all arrived item types $e\in A(\sigma)$, and $z_{i,e}=0$ otherwise. We verify that $\mathbf{z}$ is feasible for any realization of the arrivals. For any subset of assignments $S \subseteq \mathcal{E}$, we have:
	\[
	\begin{aligned}
		\sum_{(i,e) \in S} f_i(\{e\})\,z_{i,e} &= \sum_{i\in[n]} \frac{1-\varepsilon}{nk}\,\bigl|S_i\cap A(\sigma)\bigr| \\
		&\le \sum_{i\in [n]} \left( 1-(1-1/k)^{|S_i|} \right) \\
		&\le \sum_{i\in [n]} f_i(S_i) = g(S).
	\end{aligned}
	\]
	The first equality holds since $f_i(\{e\})=1/k$ for every item $e$, meaning the sum perfectly counts the number of \emph{distinct} arrived item types assigned to buyer $i$ in $S$. The first inequality holds because $\frac{1-\varepsilon}{nk}\ell \le 1-(1-1/k)^{\ell}$ is valid for all integers $\ell \in \{0, 1, \dots, nk\}$ for $\varepsilon = e^{-n}$, and $|S_i\cap A(\sigma)|\leq \min\{|S_i|,|A(\sigma)|\}$ with $|A(\sigma)|\leq m=nk$. The second inequality holds deterministically by the definition of $f_i$. Since $z_{i,e} \le x^*_{i,e}$ is satisfied (as $x^*_{i,e}\geq 1/n$ for every $e\in A(\sigma)$), $\mathbf{z}$ is feasible for all arrival sequences. Consequently, we have:
	\begin{eqnarray*}
		\mathbb{E}[g^1(\mathbf{x}^*)] &\ge &\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{(i,e) \in \mathcal{E}} f_i(\{e\})\,z_{i,e}\right]\\
		& = &\frac{1-\varepsilon}{nk} \sum_{i \in [n]} \mathbb{E}\left[|A(\sigma)|\right]\\
		& =  &\frac{1-\varepsilon}{k}\mathbb{E}\left[|A(\sigma)|\right]\\
		& \ge& n - o(n).
	\end{eqnarray*}
	Here, the last inequality follows from Fact \ref{cla:many-distinct-types}, which states that the expected number of distinct item types in the arrival sequence is at least $nk(1-o(1))$.
	
	Finally, consider $\mathbb{E}[g^2(\mathbf{x}^*)]$. Recall that $g^2$ evaluates, for each buyer $i$, the fractional coverage over the discrete probability space $\Omega$ of all possible realizations of the $u$-dimensional binary random vector $\mathbf{X}$. The $u$ dimensions of $\mathbf{X}$ are partitioned into $u/k$ blocks of length $k$. In every realization $\omega \in \Omega$, exactly one dimension per block is set to $1$, and the blocks are independent. Therefore, $|\Omega| = k^{u/k}$, and each realization $\omega$ has a uniform probability weight of $k^{-u/k}$.

We will show that for every buyer $i$ and realization $\omega \in \Omega$, the uniform fractional assignment $\mathbf{x}^*$ almost fully covers $\omega$. Specifically, we establish that:
\begin{equation}\label{finalterm}
	\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left\{1, \sum_{e\in \mathcal{U}:\; A_{i,e}\ni \omega} x^*_{i,e}\right\}\right] \ge 1-o(1).
\end{equation}
Fix an arbitrary buyer $i$ and realization $\omega$. Counting arrivals with multiplicity, and using $x^*_{i,e}=\min\{1,m_e(\sigma)/n\}$ together with $\min\{1,a\}+\min\{1,b\}\geq \min\{1,a+b\}$ for $a,b\geq 0$, we have
$$\min\left\{1, \sum_{e\in \mathcal{U}:\; A_{i,e}\ni \omega} x^*_{i,e}\right\} \geq \min\left\{1, \frac{1}{n}\cdot\bigl|\{t\in [m] \mid  A_{i,\sigma_t}\ni \omega\}\bigr|\right\}.$$
Hence, proving \eqref{finalterm} reduces to demonstrating that the number of arrivals $t$ covering $\omega$ (i.e., $A_{i,\sigma_t} \ni \omega$) is at least $n-o(n)$ with high probability. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the event that $|\{t\in[m]:\; A_{i,\sigma_t}\ni \omega\}| \geq n-o(n)$. Formally, we can lower-bound the expectation by conditioning on this event:
\begin{align}
	\mathbb{E}\left[\min\left\{1, \sum_{e\in \mathcal{U}:\; A_{i,e}\ni \omega} x^*_{i,e}\right\}\right] &\geq \Pr[\mathcal{C}] \cdot \min\left\{1, \frac{n-o(n)}{n}\right\} \nonumber \\
	&= \Pr[\mathcal{C}] \cdot (1-o(1)). \label{eq:expectation-bound}
\end{align}

To evaluate $\Pr[\mathcal{C}]$, we revisit how buyer valuations are constructed over the universe $\mathcal{U}$. Instead of sampling a vector $\mathbf{X}_i$ independently for each buyer $i$, we apply a random permutation to a single shared vector $\mathbf{X}$. Specifically, a random bijection $\pi_i : \mathcal{U} \to [u]$ maps the $u$ items to the $u$ dimensions of $\mathbf{X}$. The set $A_{i,e}$ associated with assigning item $e$ to buyer $i$ contains $\omega$ if and only if the coordinate $\pi_i(e)$ of $\omega$ equals $1$. Because $\omega$ contains exactly one $1$ per block, there are exactly $u/k$ item types in $\mathcal{U}$ that ``cover'' $\omega$ for buyer $i$. 

The probability that a uniformly random arrival corresponds to one of these covering item types is $\frac{u/k}{u}=\frac{1}{k}$. Over the $m=nk$ total independent arrivals, the number of covering arrivals is a binomial random variable with expectation $m \cdot \frac{1}{k} = n$. By standard concentration bounds (e.g., Chernoff), this quantity is tightly concentrated around its mean. Thus, $\Pr[\mathcal{C}] \ge 1 - o(1)$.

Substituting this probability back into \eqref{eq:expectation-bound} proves the claim in \eqref{finalterm}. Finally, summing over all $i\in[n]$ and $\omega \in \Omega$ yields $\mathbb{E}[g^2(\mathbf{x}^*)] \ge n(1-o(1)) = n-o(n)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an optimal offline allocation algorithm $ALG$. Let $y_{i,t,e}\geq 0$ be the probabilities that $ALG$ allocates buyer $i$ a copy of item $e$ at time $t$, respectively.
    The probability that item $e$ is allocated at time $t$ is precisely $\sum_i y_{i,t,e}$ (using that these are probabilities of disjoint events), which is at most the probability that item $e$ arrives at time $t$, that is $\Pr_{\sigma_t\sim\mathcal{D}_t}[\sigma_t=e]$. 
    Therefore these $y_{i,t,e}$ form a feasible solution to the above program.
    The value that a randomized (offline) algorithm with these marginal probabilities obtains from each buyer $i$ is at most $h^+_i(\mathbf{y}_{\mid \{i\}\times [m]\times \mathcal{U}})$, the maximum expected value of a set $S_i\subseteq [n]\times[m]\times \mathcal{U}$ containing only tuples $(i',t',e')$ with $i'=i$ with marginal inclusion probabilities $\mathbf{y}_{i',t',e'}$ (with the maximizing correlations).
    The lemma follows.

title: Definition
body_md:
The \emph{multilinear extension} $F:[0,1]^E\to \mathbb{R}$ of a set function $f:2^E \to \mathbb{R}$ maps any $\mathbf{x}\in [0,1]^E$ to 
        $$F(\mathbf{x})\triangleq \sum_{S\subseteq E} f(S) \prod_{e\in S} x_e \prod_{e\in E\setminus S} (1-x_e).$$

body_md:
\label{lem:rounding-quality}
    The multisets $S_i\subseteq \{i\}\times [m]\times \mathcal{U}$ allocated to buyers $i=1,\dots,n$ by the above randomized rounding algorithm satisfy $$\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i h_i(S_i)\right] \geq \sum_i H_i\left(\mathbf {y}_{\mid \{i\}\times [m]\times\mathcal{U}}\right).$$

title: Proof
body_md:
First, we note that by definition, the set $M\triangleq \{(i,t,e)\mid \textrm{$e$ allocated to $i$ at time $t$}\}$ satisfies for each  $(i,t,e)$:
        $$\Pr[(i,t,e)\in M] = \Pr_{\sigma_t\sim \mathcal{D}_t}[\sigma_t = e] \cdot \frac{y_{i,t,e}}{\Pr_{\sigma_t\sim \mathcal{D}_t}[\sigma_t = e]} = y_{i,t,e}.$$
        Next, we prove that the indicators $\mathds{1}[(i,t,e)\in M]$ are negatively associated (NA) \cite{joag1983negative}.
        This follows from the indicators $\{\mathds{1}[(i,t,e)\in M]\}_{i,e}$ 
        for fixed $t$ being NA, as their sum is deterministically at most one (the 0-1 rule \cite{dubhashi1996balls}). Moreover, these sets are independent of the same for all 
        $t' \neq t$, due to independence of arrivals and rounding in different time steps. Therefore, by closure of NA under products \cite{joag1983negative}, all these indicators across all triples 
        $(i,t,e)\in [n]\times [m]\times \mathcal{U}$ are NA.
        The claimed inequality then follows from NA implying submodular dominance \cite{christofides2004connection,qiu2022submodular}, and hence $\mathbb{E}[h_i(S_i)] \geq H_i(\mathbf{y}_{\mid \{i\}\times [m]\times \mathcal{U}})$ for each buyer $i$, and likewise for their sum, by linearity.

body_md:
We set  $k\triangleq \lceil\ln \ln n\rceil$ and $u \triangleq \lceil n^{2k/(2k-1)}\rceil$, clearly satisfying $k=\omega(1)$.
    
    Asymptotic growth relation \ref{ineq:u>>npoly(k)} is equivalent, after dividing both sides by $n$, to the starred asymptotic inequality below:
    $$n^{1/(2k-1)} = \exp(\Theta(\ln n/\ln \ln n)) \overset{(\star)}{=} \omega(\exp(\Theta(\ln \ln \ln n))).$$
    
    Relation \ref{ineq:k<<u^(1-1/k)} holds since $\ln\ln n$ is asymptotically dominated by any polynomial in $n$, and hence $k=o(\sqrt{n})$, combined with $k\geq 2$ and $u\geq n$ implying that $\sqrt{n}\leq n^{1-1/k}\leq u^{1-1/k}$.

    For relation \ref{ineq:bday-threshold}, first note that our choice of $u=\lceil n^{2k/(2k-1)}\rceil$ implies that
    $$u^{1-1/k}=\Theta(n^{((k-1)/k)\cdot (2k/(2k-1))}) = \Theta(n^{2(k-1)/(2k-1)}) = \Theta(n^{1-1/(2k-1)}).$$
    Dividing both sides of relation \ref{ineq:bday-threshold} by $n^{1-1/(2k-1)}$ and then taking the $k^{th}$ power of both sides, we find that this relation is equivalent to 
    $$n^{k/(2k-1)}=\omega(k\ln n),$$
    the latter holding since $k/(2k-1)\geq 1/2$ for all $k\geq 1$, and any polynomial in $n$, e.g., $n^{1/2}$, asymptotically dominates any poly-logarithmic function in $n$, e.g., $k\ln n = \Theta(\ln n \ln \ln n)$.

title: Proof
body_md:
By the Taylor expansion of $\ln(1-z)$ we have $k\ln (1-1/k)=-(1+O(1/k))$. Using this 
fact and $1$-Lipschitzness of $\exp(-z)$ for $z\geq 0$ (for which $\left|\frac{d}{dz}\exp(-z)\right| = \exp(-z) \leq 1)$, we get 
    \begin{align*}
        1-\left(1-\frac{1}{k}\right)^{k\cdot \left(H_c - H_{c-r}\right)} 
        & = 1-\exp(-(H_c-H_{c-r})(1+O(1/k))) \\
        & \leq1-\exp(-(H_c-H_{c-r})) + O\left(\frac{H_{c}}{k}\right) \\
        & = 1-\prod_{j=c-r+1}^c \exp(-1/j) + O\left(\frac{H_c}{k}\right) \\
        & \leq1-\prod_{j=c-r+1}^c (1-1/j) + O\left(\frac{H_c}{k}\right) \\
        & = \frac{r}{c} + O\left(\frac{1}{k}\right),
    \end{align*}
    where the first inequality used Lipschitzness, the second inequality used that $1-z\leq \exp(-z)$ for positive $z$, while the last step used that $c$ is a constant.

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an online algorithm $ALG$. By \Cref{lem:online-adv-structure}, the fractional allocation $\mathbf{x}$ output by $ALG$ decomposes as in \Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-decomposition}.
    Therefore, 
    fixing the (concave) function $\phi(a)=1-(1-1/k)^a$, we have that    
    $ALG$'s social welfare, $ALG(SW) =\mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i f_i^+(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\right]$, satisfies, by our lemmas and standard derivations:
\begin{align*}
        \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_i f_i^+(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})\right] & \leq \mathbb{E}\left[\sum_{i} \phi(\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1)\right] + o(n) & \textrm{\Cref{lem:online-iid-allocation-structure}} \\ 
        & = \sum_{r=1}^{c} \frac{n}{c} \cdot \mathbb{E}_{i\sim \mathrm{Uni}(D^{(r)})} [\phi(\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1)] + o(n)
         \\
        & \leq \sum_{r=1}^{c} \frac{n}{c} \cdot \phi\left(\mathbb{E}_{i\sim \mathrm{Uni}(D^{(r)})} \left[\|\mathbf{x}^{(i)}\|_1\right]\right)  + o(n) & \textrm{Jensen's Inequality}
      \\
        & \leq \frac{n}{c}\cdot \left(\sum_{r=1}^{c} \phi \left(k\cdot  \left(H_c - H_{c-r} \right)\right)\right)+ o(n) & \textrm{\Cref{lem:online-adv-unbalanced}} \\ 
        & \leq \frac{n}{c}\cdot\sum_{r=1}^{c}\left(\frac{r}{c}+O\left(\frac{1}{k}\right)\right) + o(n) & \textrm{\Cref{fact:1-(1-1/k)^(k*harmonicdiff)}}\\
        & = \frac{n}{c}\cdot\left(\frac{c(c+1)}{2c}\right) + O\left(\frac{n}{k}\right) + o(n) \\
        & = n\cdot\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2c} + o(1)\right). & k=\omega(1) &  \qedhere 
    \end{align*}

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix an arbitrary OSW instance and a fractional allocation $\mathbf{x}\in \mathrm{conv}(\mathcal{M}_\sigma)$. Let $\alpha$ denote the optimal probability distribution over the feasible integral assignments $S\in \mathcal{M}_\sigma$ that achieves $g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x})$. Recall that each such $S$ determines the bundles $S_i=\{e\in\mathcal{U} \mid (i,e)\in S\}$ assigned to buyers $i\in[n]$. This global distribution $\alpha$ naturally induces a marginal distribution $\alpha_i$ over the bundles $S_i$ assigned to each buyer $i$. By definition, $\sum_{S_i} \alpha_{i,S_i} = 1$, and the marginal probability of buyer $i$ receiving item $e$ satisfies $\sum_{S_i \ni e} \alpha_{i,S_i} = x^{(i)}_{e}$. Therefore, $\alpha_i$ constitutes a valid convex decomposition for buyer $i$'s individual fractional allocation $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$. Because the individual concave extension $f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ represents the maximum expected value over all valid decompositions of $\mathbf{x}^{(i)}$, it must be at least the expected value yielded by $\alpha_i$. Summing these bounds across all buyers completes the proof.
	
	To see that the inequality can be strict, consider an instance with two buyers $i, j$ and three arrivals $t \in \{1, 2, 3\}$ of distinct items. Every individual item $\sigma_t$ has a value of $1$. Buyer $i$'s valuations for larger bundles are $f_i(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}) = 2$, $f_i(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_3\}) = f_i(\{\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}) = 1.5$, and $f_i(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}) = 2$. Buyer $j$'s valuations symmetrically swap $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_3$: $f_j(\{\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}) = 2$, $f_j(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_3\}) = f_j(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}) = 1.5$, and $f_j(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}) = 2$. It is straightforward to check that these valuations are monotone and submodular. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be the uniform fractional allocation where $x_{i,\sigma_t} = x_{j,\sigma_t} = 0.5$ for all $t$; note that $\mathbf{x}\in \mathrm{conv}(\mathcal{M}_\sigma)$, as $x_{i,\sigma_t}+x_{j,\sigma_t}=1=m_{\sigma_t}(\sigma)$.
	
	Evaluating the individual extensions, the optimal distribution for $f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)})$ perfectly pairs $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, yielding $f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}) = 0.5 f_i(\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}) + 0.5 f_i(\{\sigma_3\}) = 1.5$. Symmetrically, the optimal distribution for $f^+_j(\mathbf{x}^{(j)})$ pairs $\sigma_2$ and $\sigma_3$, yielding $f^+_j(\mathbf{x}^{(j)}) = 1.5$. The sum of these individual upper bounds is $3$. 
	
	However, these optimal marginal distributions fundamentally conflict. To achieve a global expected welfare of $3$, we must place probability mass solely on valid integral partitions yielding $3$. Only two such partitions exist: either buyer $i$ gets $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}$ and $j$ gets $\{\sigma_3\}$, or buyer $i$ gets $\{\sigma_1\}$ and $j$ gets $\{\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}$. 
	
	Crucially, item $\sigma_1$ is assigned to buyer $i$ in \emph{both} solutions. If we let $p$ be the combined probability mass placed on these two optimal partitions, the marginal probability that buyer $i$ receives $\sigma_1$ is at least $p$. Since $x_{i,\sigma_1} = 0.5$, we are forced to set $p \le 0.5$. The remaining $1 - p \ge 0.5$ probability mass must fall on strictly suboptimal partitions with total welfare of at most $2.5$. Thus, the global expected welfare is strictly separated from the sum of the individual extensions:
	\begin{align*} g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x}) & \le 0.5(3) + 0.5(2.5) = 2.75 < 3 = \sum_i f^+_i(\mathbf{x}^{(i)}). \qedhere \end{align*}

label: lem:g_extensions
title: Fact

title: Proof
body_md:
We begin with the first statement, evaluating each extension on an integral allocation $\mathbf{x} = \mathds{1}_S$ for an assignment $S \subseteq \mathcal{E}$. For $g^+_\sigma(\mathds{1}_S)$, where $S\in \mathcal{M}_\sigma$, the unique probability distribution over feasible assignments that perfectly matches the integral marginals of $\mathds{1}_S$ is the deterministic distribution supported entirely on $S$, naturally yielding $g^+_\sigma(\mathds{1}_S) = g(S)$.
	
	For $g^1(\mathds{1}_S)$, the marginal constraints $0 \le z_{i,e} \le (\mathds{1}_S)_{i,e}$ strictly force $z_{i,e} = 0$ for all $(i,e) \notin S$. Let $S_i=\{e \mid (i,e)\in S\}$ denote the set of items assigned to buyer $i$. The resulting linear program reduces to:
$$
\begin{aligned}
g^1(\mathds{1}_S) \triangleq \max \quad &\sum_{(i,e)\in S} f_i(\{e\}) z_{i,e} \\
\text{s.t.} \quad & \sum_{(i,e)\in S'} f_i(\{e\}) z_{i,e} \le g(S') \qquad \forall S'\subseteq S, \\
& 0 \le z_{i,e} \le 1 \qquad \forall (i,e)\in S.
\end{aligned}
$$
	Clearly, the maximum value is at most $g(S)$ due to the packing constraint for $S'=S$. Because $g(S) = \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(S_i)$, the objective and constraints completely decouple across individual buyers, rendering this equivalent to the standard polymatroid LP for each buyer's submodular function $f_i$. It is a well-known property of polymatroids that the greedy algorithm---which orders the elements of $S_i$ as $e_1,\dots,e_\ell$ and sets $f_i(\{e_j\})\,z_{i,e_j}$ equal to the marginal contribution $f_i(\{e_1,\dots,e_j\})-f_i(\{e_1,\dots,e_{j-1}\})$---yields a feasible solution that perfectly achieves the upper bound $g(S)$. Here, $0\le z_{i,e_j}\le 1$, since by monotonicity and submodularity this marginal contribution lies in $[0, f_i(\{e_j\})]$; in particular, if $f_i(\{e_j\})=0$ the marginal contribution is also $0$, and we set $z_{i,e_j}=0$.
	
	For $g^2(\mathds{1}_S)$, let $c(\omega, S_i) = \sum_{e\in S_i:\; A_{i,e}\ni \omega} 1$ denote the number of times realization $\omega$ is covered by $S_i$ in buyer $i$'s valuation. Because $c(\omega, S_i)$ is an integer, $\min\{1, c(\omega, S_i)\} = \mathds{1}(c(\omega, S_i) \ge 1)$. Thus,
	\[ g^2(\mathds{1}_S) = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \frac{1}{k^{u/k}} \min\{1, c(\omega, S_i)\} = \sum_{i=1}^n \sum_{\omega \in \Omega} \frac{1}{k^{u/k}} \mathds{1}(c(\omega, S_i) \ge 1) = \sum_{i=1}^n f_i(S_i) = g(S). \]
	
	For the second statement, consider an arbitrary fractional allocation $\mathbf{x} \in \mathrm{conv}(\mathcal{M}_\sigma)$. Let $\alpha$ denote the optimal probability distribution over feasible assignments $\mathcal{M}_\sigma$ defining the concave closure $g^+_\sigma$, such that $\sum_{S \in \mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S \mathds{1}_S = \mathbf{x}$ and $g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \sum_{S \in \mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S g(S)$.
	
	Since $g^1$ is concave, applying Jensen's inequality to the convex decomposition defined by $\alpha$ yields:
	\[ g^1(\mathbf{x}) = g^1\left( \sum_{S \in \mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S \mathds{1}_S \right) \ge \sum_{S \in \mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S g^1(\mathds{1}_S) = \sum_{S \in \mathcal{M}_\sigma} \alpha_S g(S) = g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x}). \]
	An identical application of Jensen's inequality for the concave function $g^2$ yields $g^2(\mathbf{x}) \ge g^+_\sigma(\mathbf{x})$, completing the proof.

label: obs:not-online-roundable
title: Observation
body_md:
\label{obs:not-online-roundable}
	The concave closure $g^+_\sigma$ is not online-roundable, even for a simple instance with two buyers.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider an instance with two identical buyers and three sequentially arriving items. Singletons have value $1$. Bundles of size two have value $1.5$, except the specific bundle $\{\sigma_1,\sigma_2\}$, which has value $2 - \varepsilon$ for some $0 < \varepsilon < 0.5$. The full bundle has value $2 - \varepsilon/2$. It is straightforward to check that this valuation is monotone and submodular. Let $\mathbf{x}$ be the uniform fractional solution setting $x_{i,\sigma_t} = 0.5$ for both buyers $i$ and all arrivals $t \in \{1,2,3\}$.
	
	After the first two arrivals, the unique distribution optimizing $g^+_\sigma$ assigns one item to each buyer, yielding an expected welfare of $1+1=2$ (since bundling them yields only $2-\varepsilon < 2$). To successfully track $g^+_\sigma$, any online rounding algorithm must therefore irrevocably assign $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ to different buyers.
	
	When item $\sigma_3$ arrives, the ex-post optimal distribution for $g^+_\sigma$ shifts to bundling $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$ for one buyer while giving $\sigma_3$ to the other. This new configuration yields an expected welfare of $0.5((2-\varepsilon) + 1) + 0.5(1 + (2-\varepsilon)) = 3-\varepsilon$. However, because the online integral algorithm already separated $\sigma_1$ and $\sigma_2$, it is forced to bundle $\sigma_3$ with one of the previously separated items. This leads to a maximum possible expected welfare of $1.5 + 1 = 2.5$. Because $\varepsilon < 0.5$, we have $2.5 < 3-\varepsilon$. Thus, the online algorithm strictly fails to match the value of $g^+_\sigma$, completing the proof.

label: lem:approximate-or-separate
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:approximate-or-separate}
        Let $f\colon 2^{E} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}_+$ be a normalized monotone submodular function, $\mathcal{P}\subseteq [0,1]^E$ be a separable polytope with $|E|=n$, and $ALG$ be a cutting plane method using  $T$ or fewer separation queries. Then, for any $\varepsilon>0$ there is an algorithm that outputs a vector $\mathbf{y}\in \mathcal{P}$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}[F(\mathbf{y})]\geq (1-1/e-O(\varepsilon))\cdot \max_{\mathbf{z}\in \mathcal{P}}f^+(\mathbf{z})$.
        The algorithm requires $\tilde{O}(T)$ separation oracle queries to $\mathcal{P}$,
        and  $\tilde{O}({n \cdot T}\cdot {\varepsilon^{-2}})$ value oracle queries to $f$, where $\tilde{O}$ hides polylogarithmic terms in $n,T$ and~$1/\varepsilon$.

title: Remark

\cite{buchbinder2025chasing} assert that their output point $\mathbf{z}\in \mathcal{P}$ satisfies the stronger guarantee
    $$\mathbb{E}[F(\mathbf{z})] \geq (1-1/e-\varepsilon)\max_{\mathbf{x}\in \mathcal{P}}f^*(\mathbf{x}).$$
